Solvers, convergence, and reusable work

One objective · several numerical methods · explicit resource costs Solver choice is explicit. Quadratic objectives admit a linear solve; smooth logistic objectives admit Newton-CG; ADMM also supports the nonsmooth L1 penalty. AutoSolver() is an explicit, documented selection policy rather than a hidden change to the objective. This notebook compares converged solutions, opens the ADMM diagnostics, and separates factorization reuse from warm-start reuse. All comparisons below use the same prepared dataset and objective.

data.text/html:
Every compatible solver minimizes ||[ \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \ell_i(\theta_{g_i}) +\lambda_1\lVert M_1\theta\rVert_1 +\frac{\lambda_2}{2}\lVert M_2\theta\rVert_2^2 +\frac{\gamma}{2}\theta^T L\theta. ||]The feature masks state which coefficients receive each penalty. ADMM keeps copies for the sample loss, local penalties, and graph quadratic, then enforces consensus. These copies form one product-space variable in a two-block consensus formulation. The local proximal update is soft thresholding and shrinkage. The graph update solves a positive-definite linear system. Logistic loss needs an iterative inner solve; its certified proximal-error bound is plotted against the requested accuracy.
ADMM(atol=1e-6, rtol=1e-5)
QuadraticSolver(linear_solver=DirectSolve())
QuadraticSolver(linear_solver=ConjugateGradient())
NewtonSolver()
AutoSolver()  # explicit deterministic selection policy
CVXPYSolver()  # optional small-problem reference

Compare solution quality and source passes as well as wall time.

data.text/markdown:
ADMM's raw objective need not decrease on every iteration. A flat objective alone is not a convergence certificate: primal agreement, dual progress, and adequately solved inner problems are checked together. The loss is a global sample mean. Every solver includes the same local and graph terms, with the same coefficient masks. Unsupported objectives are rejected rather than silently dropping penalties.

Warm starts and factorization caches are different

The next three runs solve exactly the same prepared problem. The first starts with a new cache; the second uses a fresh session sharing the cache; the third reuses the first session's solution as well. A new session is the explicit way to start without the previous optimization history.
